title: Brainstem Localization (Midbrain, Pons, Medulla)
subtitle: Anatomy, vascular territories, cranial nerve topodiagnosis, and classical stroke syndromes of the brainstem

coreAnatomy.title: Three Laminae & Gates Rule of 4 Principles

points.text: Cross section demonstrates three laminae: the tectum, tegmentum, and basis conveying corticofugal motor pathways.
points.quote: any cross section demonstrates three laminae: the tectum, tegmentum, and basis

points.text: The basis mesencephali, basis pontis, and medullary pyramids convey the corticospinal and corticopontine motor pathways.
points.quote: convey the corticofugal motor pathways consisting of the corticospinal tract and the corticopontine tracts

points.text: The rule of 4 proposed by Gates is a didactic method for brainstem anatomy and vascular syndromes.
points.quote: rule of 4 of the brainstem proposed by Gates is a simplified and useful didactic method

points.text: In caudal medulla, 75% to 90% of corticospinal fibers decussate to form the lateral corticospinal tract.
points.quote: nearly 75% to 90% of the corticospinal fibers in the pyramid cross the ventral midline

points.text: Paramedian arteries penetrate the ventral surface to supply midline structures.
points.quote: paramedian arteries, which penetrate the ventral brainstem surface and supply the midline structures

points.text: Short circumferential arteries traverse laterally to penetrate ventrolateral and lateral surfaces.
points.quote: short circumferential arteries, which traverse laterally on the brainstem and penetrate its ventrolateral

points.text: Long circumferential arteries course around the brainstem to supply posterior structures and cerebellum.
points.quote: long circumferential arteries, which course around the brainstem and supply its posterior structures

points.text: Anterior spinal artery supplies the paramedian medulla including pyramid, medial lemniscus, and CN XII.
points.quote: anterior spinal artery supplies the paramedian region of the medulla oblongata, which includes the ipsilateral pyramid

points.text: Abducens nucleus lies in the dorsomedial pons beneath the floor of the fourth ventricle.
points.quote: abducens nerve (cranial nerve VI), which is located in the dorsomedial pons just beneath the floor

points.text: Paramedian pontine reticular formation (PPRF) lies ventromedial to abducens nucleus, driving horizontal saccades.
points.quote: Ventromedial to the abducens nucleus is the paramedian pontine reticular formation

points.text: The basis pontis contains longitudinal descending corticospinal tracts plus pontine nuclei.
points.quote: A unilateral lesion (vascular or neoplastic) of the ventrocaudal pons may involve the basis pontis

points.text: Trochlear nerve (CN IV) nucleus is in ventral central gray at inferior colliculus level.
points.quote: trochlear nerve (cranial nerve IV) is located in the ventral part of the central gray matter at the level of the inferior colliculus

points.text: Oculomotor nucleus lies beneath superior colliculus, posterior to medial longitudinal fasciculus.
points.quote: cranial nerve III) lies rostral to the trochlear nucleus beneath the superior colliculus, just posterior to the medial longitudinal

points.text: Lesions affecting the ventromedial midbrain crus cerebri damage pyramidal fibers and CN III fascicles.
points.quote: lesion affecting the cerebral peduncle, especially the ventromedial midbrain, may damage pyramidal fibers and the fascicle

localizationRules.explanation: An ipsilateral cranial nerve palsy combined with contralateral motor or sensory long-tract signs definitively places the lesion in the brainstem at the exit level of that nerve.
localizationRules.quote: protruded tongue deviates toward the lesion (away from the hemiplegia)

localizationRules.rule: Medial vs. Lateral Medullary Sensory Discriminator
localizationRules.explanation: Medial medullary lesions disrupt position and vibratory sensation (medial lemniscus), while lateral medullary lesions impair facial and body pain/temperature (spinothalamic and trigeminal).
localizationRules.quote: Contralateral loss of position and vibratory sensation (due to involvement of the medial lemniscus)

localizationRules.rule: Horner Syndrome from Lateral Tegmental Lesions
localizationRules.explanation: Ipsilateral Horner syndrome results from interruption of uncrossed descending sympathetic fibers coursing in the lateral tegmentum.
localizationRules.quote: Ipsilateral Horner syndrome (due to affection of the descending sympathetic fibers)

localizationRules.explanation: A fascicle lesion causes isolated ipsilateral lateral rectus paresis; an abducens nucleus lesion paralyzes conjugate horizontal gaze toward the lesion side.
localizationRules.quote: Ipsilateral lateral rectus paresis (cranial nerve VI)

localizationRules.rule: Ventral vs. Dorsal Midbrain Fascicular Signs
localizationRules.explanation: Ventral CN III fascicle involvement causes contralateral hemiplegia (Weber); dorsal tegmental extension involves the red nucleus and superior cerebellar peduncle causing tremor and ataxia (Benedikt, Claude).
localizationRules.quote: dorsal red nucleus and brachium conjunctivum (Claude syndrome) but with prominent cerebellar signs

keySyndromes.name: Dejerine Medial Medullary Syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Ipsilateral tongue deviation + Contralateral hemiplegia (face spared) + Contralateral vibration/position loss
keySyndromes.clue: Anterior spinal artery or vertebral artery occlusion affecting pyramid, medial lemniscus, and hypoglossal nerve.
keySyndromes.quote: medullary infarction and lateral medullary infarction (Wallenberg syndrome). CN, cranial nerve. Lateral Bulbar Branches

keySyndromes.name: Millard-Gubler Syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Ipsilateral peripheral facial palsy + Ipsilateral lateral rectus palsy + Contralateral hemiplegia
keySyndromes.clue: Ventrolateral pontine lesion involving basis pontis, exiting CN VI and CN VII fascicles, with preserved horizontal conjugate gaze.
keySyndromes.quote: A unilateral lesion (vascular or neoplastic) of the ventrocaudal pons may involve the basis pontis

keySyndromes.name: Raymond Syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Ipsilateral lateral rectus paresis (CN VI) + Contralateral hemiplegia with facial sparing
keySyndromes.clue: Ventral medial pontine lesion sparing the facial nerve fascicle and PPRF.
keySyndromes.quote: lesion of the ventral medial pons, which affects the ipsilateral abducens nerve fascicles and the corticospinal tract

keySyndromes.name: Foville Syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Ipsilateral conjugate horizontal gaze paralysis + Ipsilateral peripheral facial palsy + Contralateral hemiplegia
keySyndromes.clue: Dorsal caudal pontine tegmentum lesion involving CN VI nucleus/PPRF, facial fascicle, and corticospinal tract.
keySyndromes.quote: lesions involving the dorsal pontine tegmentum in the caudal third of the pons

keySyndromes.name: Weber Syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Ipsilateral oculomotor (CN III) palsy + Contralateral spastic hemiplegia (including lower face)
keySyndromes.clue: Ventromedial midbrain crus cerebri infarction typically from PCA or basilar bifurcation peduncular perforators.
keySyndromes.quote: results in the Weber syndrome, which consists of the following: 1. Contralateral hemiplegia (including lower facial weakness)

keySyndromes.name: Benedikt Syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Ipsilateral CN III palsy + Contralateral choreoathetosis, hemiataxia, and intention tremor
keySyndromes.clue: Midbrain tegmentum lesion affecting exiting CN III fascicle, red nucleus, and superior cerebellar peduncle.

keySyndromes.triad: Ipsilateral CN III palsy + Contralateral cerebellar ataxia (without hemiballismus)
keySyndromes.clue: Dorsal midbrain tegmentum lesion involving dorsal red nucleus and decussation of superior cerebellar peduncle.

keySyndromes.name: Locked-In Syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Quadriplegia + Aphonia + Preserved vertical eye movements and consciousness
keySyndromes.clue: Bilateral ventral pontine infarction (basilar artery thrombosis) sparing midbrain reticular activating system and supranuclear vertical gaze.

keySyndromes.name: Opalski Submedullary Syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Wallenberg lateral medullary signs + Ipsilateral hemiplegia
keySyndromes.clue: Caudal extension of lateral medullary lesion below the pyramidal decussation affecting uncrossed corticospinal fibers.
keySyndromes.quote: Opalski (Submedullary) Syndrome When ipsilateral hemiplegia is associated with symptoms of a lateral medullary syndrome

keySyndromes.name: Nothnagel Variant Syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Ipsilateral or bilateral CN III palsy + Prominent cerebellar ataxia
keySyndromes.clue: Dorsal midbrain syndrome variant affecting tectum/tegmentum and brachium conjunctivum.
keySyndromes.quote: Nothnagel syndrome is a variant of the dorsal midbrain syndrome and has been described as unilateral or bilateral oculomotor

boardTraps.text: Opalski syndrome causes IPSILATERAL hemiparesis because the lesion extends caudally below the pyramidal decussation, damaging post-decussation corticospinal fibers.

boardTraps.text: Abducens nucleus lesions cause complete conjugate horizontal gaze paralysis toward the lesion; fascicle lesions cause isolated lateral rectus abduction weakness with preserved conjugate gaze.

boardTraps.text: In medial medullary syndrome (Dejerine), the protruding tongue deviates toward the lesion and away from the hemiplegic side.
